title.en: Separate the vector from its coordinates

summary: Show that a change of basis relabels a fixed geometric object, while a transformation moves it.
objective: Prevent the common conflation of changing coordinates with changing the world.
applies_when: Two bases, frames or coordinate systems appear in the same scene.
Coordinates are displayed for a vector, point or pose.
The user can switch between a world view and a local or camera view.
intent_signals: show the same vector in another basis
example_prompts: Show one vector with its coordinates in two different bases.
Switch to the object frame without moving anything.
negative_signals: Single-frame scenes where no alternative coordinates are shown.
Cases where the object really is being transformed, which is the opposite operation.
not_for: Single-frame scenes where no alternative coordinates are shown.
Cases where the object really is being transformed, which is the opposite operation.

principles: A vector is determined by the linear combination of basis vectors that produces it, so the same geometric arrow has different coordinate triples in different bases while remaining the same arrow.
Changing basis and applying a transformation can produce identical numeric changes, which is why the scene must show which one occurred.
A scene that animates the object when the basis changes teaches that coordinates are the object, which is the misconception the demonstration should remove.
The distinction becomes practical wherever frames stack: camera, object and world coordinates are the same points described differently.
implementation: Keep geometry in one reference representation and compute displayed coordinates per basis, rather than storing coordinates and reinterpreting them.
On a basis change, animate the axes and the grid while the object stays fixed in space, and say so on screen.
Show both coordinate triples at once during the transition so the viewer sees two descriptions of one object.
Provide the paired demonstration: the same numeric change produced by a transformation, with the object moving and the axes fixed.
Label every coordinate readout with the basis it is expressed in.
observable_checks: Change basis and confirm the object does not move relative to other fixed geometry.
Confirm both coordinate readouts are labelled with their basis and update simultaneously.
Apply a transformation and a basis change that produce the same numbers and confirm the scene distinguishes them.

Convert to the second basis and back and confirm the coordinates return within a tolerance chosen for the scale and conditioning of the two bases; a skewed or nearly singular basis loses digits, so exact equality is the wrong test in floating point.

creative_affordances: Presentation of the two descriptions, whether side by side, ghosted or as an animated relabelling, is a free design choice.
Non-orthogonal and skewed bases make the point more strongly and are worth showing.
known_limits: Authored conceptual guidance citing the basis-combination definition; it does not derive change-of-basis matrices.
Affine frames with a translated origin add a component not covered here.

claims.statement: A vector is expressed as a linear combination of basis vectors, and the transformation of that vector follows the same combination of the images of the basis vectors, so the coordinates describe the vector relative to a chosen basis rather than being the vector itself.
claims.scope: Finite-dimensional vector spaces with a chosen basis; affine translation is not included.
